title: Equality and discrimination at work
summary: The protected characteristics, the four forms of discrimination, what protection covers at work, and where to get help.

sections.title: The Equality Act 2010
sections.body:
The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination. At work, that protection covers how people are recruited, paid, promoted, trained, dismissed and made redundant.
The same Act protects people in other settings too, such as education, public services and buying or renting property.
key_points: The Equality Act 2010 is the law that protects people from discrimination
Protection at work covers recruitment, pay, promotion, training, dismissal and redundancy

sections.title: Protected characteristics
sections.body:
The Act protects people with protected characteristics. These are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage or civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation.
Protection also reaches people who are linked to someone with a protected characteristic, such as a family member or friend.
key_points: Protected characteristics include age, disability, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation
People linked to someone with a protected characteristic are also protected

sections.title: The four forms of discrimination
sections.body:
The Act recognises four forms of discrimination: direct discrimination, indirect discrimination, harassment and victimisation.
Direct discrimination is treating someone worse because of a protected characteristic. Indirect discrimination is a rule or practice that puts people with a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage.
key_points: Direct discrimination treats someone worse because of a protected characteristic
Indirect discrimination puts people at a particular disadvantage through a rule or practice
Harassment and victimisation are also forms of discrimination

sections.title: Victimisation and speaking up
sections.body:
Victimisation is treating someone badly because they complained about discrimination, or because they supported someone else's claim.
People who speak up are protected from this. Raising a concern in good faith is part of keeping the workplace fair.
key_points: Victimisation is treating someone badly for complaining or supporting a claim
People who speak up are protected

sections.title: Reasonable adjustments and positive action
sections.body:
Employers should make reasonable adjustments for disabled staff and applicants. This can apply at any stage, from applying for a job to the day-to-day work.
The law also allows positive action for people who are at a disadvantage, have particular needs, or are under-represented in a type of work.
key_points: Reasonable adjustments are expected for disabled staff and applicants
Positive action is allowed for people at a disadvantage or under-represented

sections.title: Where to get help
sections.body:
A concern can be raised with the organisation first. Mediation, advice from Acas or Citizens Advice, and a claim to a court or an employment tribunal are all possible routes.
The GOV.UK page on discrimination sets out these routes. Read it for the detail.
key_points: Raise the concern with the organisation first
Acas and Citizens Advice can help
A claim can be made to a court or an employment tribunal

questions.prompt: Which of these is a protected characteristic?
questions.explanation: Religion or belief is a protected characteristic. Hobbies and favourite teams are not.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the four forms of discrimination the Act recognises?
questions.explanation: Direct discrimination is one of the four forms, with indirect discrimination, harassment and victimisation.

options: Someone who complains about discrimination or supports someone else's claim
questions.explanation: Victimisation is treating someone badly for complaining or supporting a claim, and the Act protects people who do either.

questions.prompt: What should an employer make for a disabled member of staff?
options: Nothing; the law does not require it
questions.explanation: Employers should make reasonable adjustments for disabled staff and applicants.

questions.prompt: Where can a person get help with a discrimination concern?
options: From Acas or Citizens Advice, or by a tribunal claim
questions.explanation: Acas and Citizens Advice can help, and a claim can be made to a court or an employment tribunal.
